source.title: Information Geometry of Orthogonal Initializations and Training

record.file_problem: Text appears complete; no garbling or cutoff evident.
record.tranche_reason: Compares initialization and weight-constraint settings using training-loss and test-accuracy curves, bearing on initialization effects but not the versions’ central training-classification-error claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports training loss and test accuracy for 200-layer tanh networks on CIFAR-10 and SVHN. It does not report training classification error, so these results do not test V1. Other versions concern settings not varied here. Values are shown only in figures; prose describes qualitative comparisons. The cited findings from earlier studies are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares initialization-dependent training-loss trajectories in 200-layer, width-400 tanh networks. These results test V4; training classification error is not required for that version. The study is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors also derive a connection between Jacobian spectrum and a bound on FIM curvature. They argue that greater initial isometry does not guarantee faster subsequent training because curvature changes during optimization. Manifold-constrained networks are less sensitive to initial smoothness, and their loss-reduction rate is not explained by that smoothness.
record.recipe_differences: Uses 200-layer tanh networks with critical initializations on CIFAR-10 and SVHN, comparing Euclidean training with Stiefel and Oblique manifold optimization; it does not reproduce the claim’s training-classification-error evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset (CIFAR-10 versus SVHN), q* initialization, and Euclidean versus Stiefel or Oblique optimization are varied; the paper describes differences in training loss and accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Stiefel and Oblique optimization reduce training loss faster than Euclidean optimization and are insensitive to the two tested q* initializations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Maintaining orthogonal or nearly orthogonal weights during training can reduce sensitivity to initialization and accelerate loss reduction.

fits_no_version.finding: Initial maximum FIM eigenvalue correlates with maximum squared Jacobian singular value, but FIM smoothness does not predict manifold optimization speed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initial Jacobian geometry relates to curvature, but curvature alone does not explain optimization speed across training procedures.

record.problems: Training-loss and test-accuracy outcomes are presented in figures without numeric values in the text. The study trains five networks of each kind, but does not report uncertainty intervals for the performance curves. It does not measure training classification error.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure-only qualitative outcomes are discussed in the text but cannot be assigned to the claim versions because the versions require training classification error or specific other settings not measured here.

untested.parts: Training classification error in convolutional networks, including corrupted labels, is not measured.
Teacher-student ReLU networks, extra width, and spurious local minima are not tested.
Depth comparisons, identity shortcuts, and residual training without normalization are not tested.
No trainable-depth sweep, activation-function comparison, Gaussian-versus-orthogonal training comparison at matched variance, or 10,000-layer convolutional experiment.
Learning rates relative to a stability threshold, catapult recovery, and edge-of-stability dynamics are not tested.
No batch-normalization intervention or Fixup comparison. Discussion of normalization mechanisms does not test its claimed training advantage.

missing.what: Extract qualitative training-loss comparisons for both datasets: Euclidean q* ≈ 9×10^-4 performs worse than q* = 1/64. Both initializations are critical, with mean squared Jacobian singular value set to one. Numerical curve values are unnecessary to record the explicitly stated comparison.

Record the qualification that the more isometric Euclidean initialization undergoes a more pronounced early increase in maximum FIM eigenvalue, associated with an inflection in training loss. This is a proposed explanation, not demonstrated causation.

record.verdict_notes: The extraction incorrectly treats training classification error as necessary for every version. V4 concerns learning speed, so the reported training-loss comparisons bear directly on it. Figure 1's caption conflicts with Section 4.2 about which Euclidean initialization attains the highest test accuracy; the verdict uses the explicit training-loss comparison in the prose.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, model size, and early stopping are not reported as outcomes.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima, and width comparisons are not studied.
Plain versus residual shortcut depth comparisons and normalization removal are not studied.

The study compares critical initializations with different q* and manifold-constrained training, but does not compare orthogonal and Gaussian weights of the same variance, or test trainable depth across depths. Figure-only training-loss curves are described qualitatively in the text; no classification-error result is given.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, catapult dynamics, and sharpness during training are not tested.
Batch normalization is not added or compared with Fixup.

relationships.condition: Unconstrained Euclidean training of 200-layer tanh networks on CIFAR-10 and SVHN
relationships.reason: Section 4.2 and Figure 1 report worse training-loss performance at q* ≈ 9×10^-4 than at q* = 1/64, despite the former having a more isometric initial Jacobian. Initial signal preservation alone does not order training speed. Based on text; the record contains no rows.
relationships.display_finding: Training loss was worse at q* ≈ 9×10^-4 than at q* = 1/64, despite a more isometric initial Jacobian.
